title: Getting Started with Playwright and TypeScript
excerpt: New to Playwright? This guide will help you build a strong foundation using TypeScript. You'll learn why TypeScript is the preferred choice for automation, understand the language features you'll use every day, and write your first pieces of Playwright-ready code.
html:
Getting Started: Part 1

If you're planning to learn browser automation, Playwright is one of the best places to start. It's fast, reliable, open source, and supports all major browsers with a single API.

One question many beginners ask is:

Should I learn Playwright with JavaScript or TypeScript?

Although Playwright supports both, most companies and experienced automation engineers prefer TypeScript. It helps you write cleaner code, catch mistakes early, and makes large automation projects much easier to maintain.

In this article, we'll cover the basics of TypeScript that every Playwright beginner should know before writing their first automated test.

Let's get started.

Why TypeScript Instead of JavaScript?

JavaScript is a flexible language, but that flexibility sometimes works against you. Since JavaScript doesn't enforce data types, small mistakes can go unnoticed until you actually run your test.

Consider this example.

JavaScript

const timeout = "5000";

await page.waitForTimeout(timeout);

At first glance, this looks fine. However, waitForTimeout() expects a number, not a string. JavaScript won't complain while you're writing the code, so you may only discover the issue when the test runs.

Now compare it with TypeScript.

TypeScript

const timeout: number = 5000;

await page.waitForTimeout(timeout);

Here, TypeScript immediately understands that timeout must be a number. If you accidentally assign a string, your editor will highlight the mistake before you even run the test.

This early feedback saves time and prevents many common bugs.

Some of the biggest advantages of using TypeScript are:

  • Better code completion in your editor

  • Detects mistakes before execution

  • Easier to refactor large projects

  • More readable and maintainable code

Better collaboration when working in teams

If you're only writing a few small scripts, JavaScript is perfectly fine. But if your goal is to build a real automation framework or work as a QA Automation Engineer, learning TypeScript is well worth the effort.

TypeScript Basics Every Automation Engineer Should Know

The good news is that you don't need to become a TypeScript expert before learning Playwright.

In fact, you'll probably use only a small portion of the language every day. Let's look at the concepts you'll encounter most often.

Understanding const, let, and var

Before creating variables, it's important to understand how they are declared.

In modern TypeScript, you'll mainly use const and let. Although var still exists, it's considered outdated and is rarely used in modern projects.

const

Use const when the value shouldn't be reassigned.

const username = "john@example.com";

This is the most common way to declare variables in Playwright tests because values like URLs, usernames, passwords, selectors, and configuration settings usually don't change during a test.

If you try to reassign it:

const username = "john@example.com";

username = "alice@example.com";

TypeScript will immediately report an error because const variables cannot be reassigned.

Use const whenever possible. It makes your code safer and easier to understand.

let

Use let when the value needs to change later.

let attempts = 0;

attempts++;

console.log(attempts);

You'll typically use let for:

  • Counters

  • Loops

  • Values that change during execution

  • Temporary variables

If a variable is expected to change, let is the right choice.

var

You may still see older tutorials using var.

var username = "john@example.com";

While this code works, var has different scoping rules that can lead to unexpected behavior in larger applications.

Because of this, modern TypeScript and JavaScript projects almost always avoid var.

As a beginner, you can safely follow this simple rule:

  • Use const by default.

  • Use let only when the value needs to change.

  • Avoid var in new code.

Variables

Variables store information that your tests can use later.

const username: string = "john@example.com";
const retries: number = 3;
const isLoggedIn: boolean = false;

Here we're defining three different types of data.

  • string stores text.

  • number stores numeric values.

  • boolean stores either true or false.

You'll use these types constantly when working with login credentials, counters, feature flags, API responses, and configuration values.

Although TypeScript can often figure out the type automatically, writing it explicitly is a great way to learn and makes your code easier to understand.

Arrays

An array stores multiple values of the same type.

const users: string[] = [
  "John",
  "Alice",
  "Michael"
];

Instead of creating three separate variables, you can keep them together in one collection.

Arrays are useful for:

  • Multiple test users

  • Search keywords

  • Product names

  • Email addresses

  • Test data

You'll work with arrays frequently when writing data-driven tests.

Functions

Functions allow you to reuse code instead of writing the same logic repeatedly.

function greet(name: string): string {
  return `Hello ${name}`;
}

Let's break this down.

  • name: string means the function expects text.

  • : string after the brackets means the function returns text.

If you call the function like this:

greet("John");

It returns:

Hello John

Functions make your code easier to organize and reduce duplication.

Arrow Functions

You'll see arrow functions everywhere in Playwright.

const greet = (name: string): string => {
  return `Hello ${name}`;
};

This does exactly the same thing as the previous example. It's simply a newer syntax that's widely used in modern JavaScript and TypeScript.

Don't worry if it looks unfamiliar at first. After writing a few tests, it quickly becomes second nature.

Interfaces

Interfaces define the structure of an object.

Imagine every test user in your project must have an email and password.

interface User {
  email: string;
  password: string;
}

Now you can create objects that follow this structure.

const user: User = {
  email: "john@example.com",
  password: "Password123"
};

If you accidentally forget a required property or assign the wrong data type, TypeScript immediately warns you.

Interfaces become incredibly useful as your project grows. They're commonly used for:

  • Test data

  • API request bodies

  • API responses

  • User models

  • Configuration objects

You don't need to master interfaces today, but it's worth becoming comfortable with them early.

Understanding Async and Await

This is one of the most important concepts in Playwright.

Every browser action takes time.

Opening a webpage...

Clicking a button...

Waiting for an element...

Submitting a form...

These actions don't happen instantly. The browser needs time to complete them.

That's why most Playwright commands are asynchronous.

You'll often see code like this:

await page.goto("https://example.com");

await page.fill("#email", "john@example.com");

await page.click("button");

The await keyword tells Playwright:

"Wait until this action finishes before moving to the next line."

Without await, your test may try to interact with elements before the page is ready, leading to unpredictable failures.

As a beginner, here's a simple rule to remember:

If you're calling a Playwright action, there's a good chance it needs await.

Over time, this will become second nature.

Practice Before Moving On

Before writing your first Playwright test, spend a little time getting comfortable with these TypeScript concepts.

Try creating a simple .ts file and practice the following:

  • Create variables using string, number, and boolean.

  • Create an array of five usernames.

  • Write a function that returns a welcome message.

  • Create an interface for a user with a name, email, and password.

  • Create an object that follows your interface.

These exercises may seem simple, but they'll make learning Playwright much easier.
